title: A New Human-Likeness and Comfort Index for Robot Movements Along Prescribed Paths
comment: 14 pages, 5 figures, accepted for IEEE Transactions on Cybernetics
summary: As human-robot interaction rapidly spreads in numerous fields, the subject of robot acceptance gains increasing importance. Visual similarity to the human body, as occurs for humanoids, is generally not enough to ensure acceptance in physical interaction, as acceptance directly links to comfort and ergonomics, which are measured in terms of the quality of the robot movement perceived by the human. This paper discusses the connection between comfort and similarity of the robot movement to the human one. By considering the kinematic characterization of human movement, this paper focuses on the time laws of such movements, wherein the end-effector path is prescribed. Based on the lognormality principle for modeling human movements, a human-likeness index is defined and used to provide an a priori characterization of trajectories. Such an index can be used to evaluate the performance of trajectory generation algorithms in producing human-like movements before they are actually executed. For validation purposes, 68 subjects are required to judge their comfort. The results of three experimental campaigns involving a physical interaction with a robot demonstrate a globally consistent trend between the preference in terms of perceived comfort and the distribution of the suggested human-likeness index.

AI.tldr: This paper defines a human-likeness index based on the lognormality principle to characterize robot trajectories and evaluates its correlation with human-perceived comfort during physical interaction, demonstrating that comfort preference aligns with the index values.
AI.motivation: Visual similarity alone is insufficient to ensure robot acceptance in physical interaction; acceptance depends on comfort and ergonomics, which are measured by how humans perceive robot movement quality.
AI.method: The study investigates the relationship between comfort and movement similarity by analyzing kinematic characterization of human movement, focusing on time laws of movements with prescribed end-effector paths. Based on the lognormality principle for modeling human movements, a human-likeness index is defined to provide an a priori characterization of trajectories. This index enables evaluation of trajectory generation algorithms' performance in producing human-like movements.
AI.result: Three experimental campaigns with 68 subjects physically interacting with a robot show a globally consistent trend between perceived comfort preference and the distribution of the suggested human-likeness index.
AI.conclusion: The human-likeness index can effectively evaluate trajectory generation algorithms' performance in creating human-like movements before actual execution, providing a useful tool for assessing robot movement comfort and ergonomics.

title: Native Video-Action Pretraining for Generalizable Robot Control
summary: The advent of video-action models offers a promising path for robot control. Nevertheless, we argue that repurposing video generative models designed for digital content creation is inherently inadequate for physical environments. To bridge this gap, we present LingBot-VA 2.0, a video-action foundation model built from the ground up for embodiment. Four core design principles showcase its evolution from LingBot-VA. (1) Departing from traditional reconstruction-focused VAEs, we introduce a semantic visual-action tokenizer, which aligns visual representations with both semantics and actions, improving instruction following and action precision in subsequent policy learning. (2) Given the strictly causal nature of temporal dynamics, we adopt a causal pretraining paradigm, training from scratch to circumvent the catastrophic forgetting that frequently occurs when adapting bidirectional architectures. (3) To meet the demands of high-frequency inference, our model employs a sparse MoE backbone, expanding model capacity without compromising efficiency. (4) Real-time closed-loop control is realized through an enhanced asynchronous inference scheme, which predicts future latents in parallel with action execution while re-grounding each rollout on the latest observation via learned forward dynamics. Real-world deployment validates LingBot-VA 2.0 as a robust foundation model, as evidenced by its few-shot generalization across complex manipulation tasks.

AI.tldr: LingBot-VA 2.0 is a video-action foundation model specifically designed for robot control, addressing limitations of repurposing video generative models by introducing a semantic visual-action tokenizer, causal pretraining, sparse MoE backbone, and enhanced asynchronous inference scheme, achieving robust few-shot generalization across complex manipulation tasks.
AI.motivation: The authors argue that repurposing video generative models designed for digital content creation is inherently inadequate for physical environments, creating a gap that needs to be bridged with a model built from the ground up for embodiment.
AI.method: Four core design principles: (1) Semantic visual-action tokenizer aligning visual representations with both semantics and actions (replacing reconstruction-focused VAEs), (2) Causal pretraining paradigm for strictly causal temporal dynamics, (3) Sparse Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) backbone for high-frequency inference, (4) Enhanced asynchronous inference scheme for real-time closed-loop control with parallel latent prediction and action execution.
AI.result: Real-world deployment validates LingBot-VA 2.0 as a robust foundation model with few-shot generalization across complex manipulation tasks.
AI.conclusion: LingBot-VA 2.0 successfully demonstrates that a purpose-built video-action foundation model can achieve robust performance in embodied control tasks, overcoming the limitations of adapting video generative models for physical environments.

title: Learning Adaptive Solvers for Distributed Factor Graph Optimization on Matrix Lie Groups
summary: Modern robotic perception increasingly involves large-scale geometric optimization problems distributed across multiple robots or sessions. However, existing distributed solvers often depend on brittle hand tuning and primarily target rigid body pose graphs. To address this, we present DeepCORD, a learning-augmented framework for distributed factor graph optimization on general matrix Lie groups. By unfolding a parallel and accelerated Riemannian optimizer into differentiable iterations, DeepCORD learns a self-supervised feedback policy that dynamically adapts solver parameters according to the optimization phase and communication status. The resulting method enables adaptive distributed optimization over matrix Lie groups under both synchronous and asynchronous communication regimes. Extensive experiments on real-world $\mathrm{SE}$(3) pose graph optimization and $\mathrm{SL}$(4) projective submap alignment show that our method achieves lower objective values than existing distributed baselines on most benchmarks across realistic operating scenarios.

AI.tldr: DeepCORD is a learning-augmented framework for distributed factor graph optimization on general matrix Lie groups (e.g., SE(3), SL(4)). It learns a self-supervised feedback policy to dynamically adapt solver parameters based on optimization phase and communication status, outperforming existing distributed baselines in SE(3) pose graph optimization and SL(4) projective submap alignment.
AI.motivation: Modern robotic perception requires large-scale geometric optimization across distributed robots/sessions. Existing distributed solvers rely on brittle hand-tuning and primarily target rigid body pose graphs (SE(3)), lacking adaptability to general matrix Lie groups and communication regimes.
AI.method: DeepCORD unfolds a parallel, accelerated Riemannian optimizer into differentiable iterations and learns a self-supervised feedback policy. This policy dynamically adjusts solver parameters according to optimization phase and communication status, supporting both synchronous and asynchronous communication regimes for general matrix Lie groups.
AI.result: Extensive experiments on SE(3) pose graph optimization and SL(4) projective submap alignment demonstrate that DeepCORD achieves lower objective values than existing distributed baselines across most benchmarks in realistic operating scenarios.
AI.conclusion: DeepCORD successfully enables adaptive distributed optimization over general matrix Lie groups under both synchronous and asynchronous communication regimes, outperforming traditional distributed solvers in objective value minimization for robotic perception tasks.

title: ContactMimic: Humanoid Object Interaction via Contact Control
summary: Keypoint tracking alone is insufficient for object interaction tasks such as sitting on a chair, wiping a board, or pushing furniture, where the robot can reach the correct pose without making meaningful physical contact with the object. We present CONTACTMIMIC, a learning framework that tracks explicit partlevel binary contact commands alongside keypoint trajectories. CONTACTMIMIC is made possible through the use of contact-following rewards and a trajectory augmentation scheme aimed at breaking the correlations between keypoint trajectories and contact labels. The resulting policy successfully decouples contact behavior from keypoint geometry, and achieves precise physical contact as well as contact-controllability (produce or suppress contact during deployment as desired). Simulation experiments across 10 diverse human-object interaction motions confirm that CONTACTMIMIC exhibits contact controllability that enables it to complete manipulation tasks without task-specific rewards, while also outperforming keypoint-only trackers on contact-relevant tasks. Ablations confirm the necessity of the proposed trajectory augmentation scheme and sim2real deployment validates contact controllability in the real world across 5 different motions. Video results are available on https://lixinyao11.github.io/contactmimic-page/.

AI.tldr: CONTACTMIMIC is a learning framework that jointly tracks keypoint trajectories and part-level binary contact commands, enabling robots to achieve precise, controllable physical contact for manipulation tasks like sitting, wiping, and pushing objects.
AI.motivation: Keypoint tracking alone is insufficient for object interaction tasks where robots must make meaningful physical contact (e.g., sitting on a chair, wiping a board, pushing furniture) but can reach correct poses without contact.
AI.method: A learning framework that tracks explicit part-level binary contact commands alongside keypoint trajectories, using contact-following rewards and a trajectory augmentation scheme designed to break correlations between keypoint trajectories and contact labels.
AI.result: The resulting policy successfully decouples contact behavior from keypoint geometry, achieving precise physical contact and contact-controllability (ability to produce or suppress contact as desired). It outperforms keypoint-only trackers on contact-relevant tasks across 10 diverse motions in simulation and validates controllability in the real world across 5 different motions.
AI.conclusion: CONTACTMIMIC enables robots to complete manipulation tasks without task-specific rewards while maintaining precise physical contact, demonstrating the importance of explicit contact modeling for object interaction tasks.

title: DexVerse: A Modular Benchmark for Multi-Task, Multi-Embodiment Dexterous Manipulation
summary: Building general-purpose dexterous manipulation policies requires benchmarks that go beyond isolated tasks to systematically evaluate policies across diverse interaction modes, sensory conditions, and robot embodiments. However, existing benchmarks remain limited in task and data diversity, embodiment coverage, or controllable visual variation, hindering studies of cross-task and cross-embodiment generalization. We present DexVerse, a large-scale and modular benchmark for dexterous manipulation. DexVerse includes 100 tasks spanning a broad range of manipulation skills, including object grasping and relocation, articulated-object interaction, functional tool use, bimanual coordination, non-prehensile control, contact-rich behaviors, multi-goal execution, and long-horizon multi-stage task completion. It supports 3 robot arms and 6 dexterous hands, and is extensible to new tasks, assets, and embodiments. To evaluate visuomotor generalization, DexVerse provides configurable visual variations in textures, background, lighting, and camera viewpoints. We further provide a VR-based teleoperation interface and 3,180 demonstrations with synchronized proprioceptive, RGB, depth, point-cloud, and state observations. We benchmark representative methods, including Diffusion Policy, DP3, OpenVLA, and $π_{0.5}$, across 19 tasks. Results reveal substantial challenges in task generalization and visuomotor robustness, establishing DexVerse as a promising testbed for general-purpose dexterous manipulation. Project page: https://ycyao216.github.io/DexVerse.site

AI.tldr: DexVerse is a large-scale, modular benchmark for dexterous manipulation comprising 100 diverse tasks across multiple robot embodiments (3 arms + 6 hands), configurable visual variations, and 3,180 demonstrations with multi-modal observations. Benchmarking state-of-the-art methods reveals significant challenges in task generalization and visuomotor robustness, establishing it as a comprehensive testbed for general-purpose dexterous manipulation research.
AI.motivation: General-purpose dexterous manipulation policies require benchmarks that systematically evaluate policies across diverse interaction modes, sensory conditions, and robot embodiments. Existing benchmarks are limited in task and data diversity, embodiment coverage, and controllable visual variation, hindering studies of cross-task and cross-embodiment generalization.
AI.method: DexVerse is a large-scale, modular benchmark featuring: (1) 100 tasks spanning grasping, articulated interaction, tool use, bimanual coordination, non-prehensile control, contact-rich behaviors, multi-goal execution, and long-horizon tasks; (2) support for 3 robot arms and 6 dexterous hands; (3) configurable visual variations in textures, background, lighting, and camera viewpoints; (4) VR-based teleoperation interface; (5) 3,180 demonstrations with synchronized proprioceptive, RGB, depth, point-cloud, and state observations.
AI.result: Benchmarking representative methods (Diffusion Policy, DP3, OpenVLA, π0.5) across 19 tasks reveals substantial challenges in task generalization and visuomotor robustness, demonstrating the complexity of achieving true general-purpose dexterous manipulation capabilities.
AI.conclusion: DexVerse establishes itself as a comprehensive and promising testbed for general-purpose dexterous manipulation research, providing the necessary diversity and controllability to advance the field toward robust, cross-task, and cross-embodiment generalization.
